questions.q: Name the three components of Sternberg's Triarchic Theory and give the alternative label used in the NCERT text for each (e.g., Componential = Analytical).
questions.a: The three components are: Componential (Analytical), Experiential (Creative), and Contextual (Practical). A wrong answer that swaps labels (e.g., calling Experiential "Analytical") reveals the student has memorized the names but not their functional meanings — a common error when students treat the theory as a list rather than a process model.

questions.q: A student memorizes a new formula by linking it to a familiar physics derivation, plans which problems to practice first, and then solves them quickly. Identify which sub-component of Componential intelligence each action represents.
questions.a: Memorizing by linking = Knowledge-acquisition component; planning practice order = Meta (higher-order) component; solving quickly = Performance component. If a student assigns "planning" to performance, they confuse executive control with execution — a critical distinction because meta-components monitor and direct performance components.

questions.q: Riya has never baked a cake. She watches a video, realizes the oven temperature in the recipe is for a conventional oven but she has a convection oven, so she reduces the temperature by 20°C and checks five minutes early. The cake is perfect. Which triarchic intelligence is primarily demonstrated? Justify in one sentence.
questions.a: Experiential (Creative) intelligence — she used past experience (watching the video) to novelly adapt the recipe for a new appliance. A wrong answer of "Componential" shows the student equates any problem-solving with analytical intelligence, missing that experiential intelligence specifically handles novelty and automation of new tasks.

questions.q: Compare how Componential and Contextual intelligence would approach the same challenge: "You have two hours to prepare for an unexpected test on a chapter you haven't read." List two distinct strategies for each.
questions.a: Componential: (1) Break chapter into sub-topics, allocate time per sub-topic, (2) Use meta-component to monitor recall after each section. Contextual: (1) Ask a classmate which topics the teacher emphasizes, focus only on those, (2) If time runs out, negotiate a retest or extra credit. A response that lists only study techniques for both reveals failure to see contextual intelligence as environment-shaping (selecting/modifying the situation) rather than task-analysis.

questions.q: Critique the claim: "Sternberg's Contextual intelligence is just 'street smarts' and therefore less important than Componential intelligence for academic success." Use evidence from the theory.
questions.a: The claim is flawed because Sternberg defines Contextual intelligence as adaptation, shaping, AND selection of environments — all vital in academics (e.g., selecting the right elective, shaping a study group, adapting to a new syllabus). Dismissing it ignores that real-world success (including academic) requires all three; the theory explicitly states they interact. A student agreeing with the claim shows a hierarchical bias from g-factor thinking, not triarchic integration.

questions.q: Design a 5-minute classroom activity that lets Class 12 students experience the difference between Experiential and Contextual intelligence. Describe the task, the expected two types of responses, and how you would debrief.
questions.a: Task: "Your group has 5 minutes to build the tallest free-standing tower using only 20 straws and tape. The tower must survive a 10-second fan blow." Experiential responses: novel structural designs (e.g., tripod base, guy-wires). Contextual responses: testing the fan early, reinforcing weak spots, or moving the tower to a sheltered corner. Debrief: label each group's actions. A poor answer describes only the building process without distinguishing novelty-use (experiential) from environment-management (contextual).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Sternberg's Triarchic Theory proposes that intelligence comprises three distinct but ______ components: Componential (analytical) intelligence for analyzing and solving problems, Experiential (creative) intelligence for using past experiences to deal with novel situations, and Contextual (practical) intelligence for adapting to, shaping, and selecting real-world environments to achieve goals.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the captain of your ______ cricket team.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) distinguish the three components with their sub-components/functions, (2) classify real-life behaviors into the correct triarchic category, and (3) explain why a single IQ score fails to capture contextual and experiential intelligence.
